CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pain in the back of the right heel extending up into the calf, worse after workouts and on first waking in the morning.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is an adult male, Dennis, presenting for the first time to this office. He is training for a triathlon and reports right posterior heel pain that radiates up into the calf. The pain is worse after workouts and when he first gets up in the morning, where it feels tight and almost like tearing. It eases after about 10 to 15 minutes of walking but returns after prolonged sitting followed by standing, and also after heavy activity.

Current training: running about 10 kilometers in the morning, cycling for 45 minutes to 1 hour at lunchtime, and swimming 30 minutes to 1 hour in the evening. He trains five days a week, alternating long runs and long bike sessions on weekends, with one day off. He does not stretch. He reports going slowly until warmed up. Pain is predominantly on the right side.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lower extremities examined. Pain with passive dorsiflexion of the right ankle (toes pulled toward the body). Mild pain with resisted plantarflexion (pushing against examiner) on the right. No pain with calf squeeze on the left or right. Thompson test negative. Significant tenderness to palpation over the right heel and along the right Achilles tendon.

RESULTS
Thompson test: negative.
No imaging performed or ordered at this time.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Achilles tendinitis, right, attributed to overuse from aggressive training for an event.
- Hold training for one to two weeks.
- Ibuprofen (Advil), 3 tablets every 6 hours, as an anti-inflammatory.
- Referral for physical therapy visits focused on strengthening and stretching instruction, with stretching to be learned before resuming activities.
- Return visit 7 to 10 days after the first physical therapy appointment to monitor progress. Office staff to schedule upon call-in.
- X-ray not indicated at this time. If pain persists about 10 days without change despite activity modification, more aggressive treatment may be considered.
- Patient agrees with plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems: depression, hypertension, and status post rotator cuff repair.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair who presents for followup of chronic problems. He reports doing pretty well over the past six months.

Depression: He has been managing his depression with new strategies rather than medication, as he is already taking multiple medications. He sees a counselor once a week and has been swimming at the pool frequently over the summer and fall. He reports his depression is going well. He does not feel the need to start medication at this time and knows he can call if he does.

Hypertension: He reports good days and bad days with his blood pressure. He takes his medication daily (Norvasc). He acknowledges occasional dietary indiscretions, including burgers, wine, and salt intake. He checks his blood pressure about once a week at a CVS pharmacy kiosk.

Rotator cuff repair: Performed about eight months ago. He reports it is doing well. He has been stretching with a yoga ball and is getting stronger. He has progressed from supervised physical therapy to home exercises only and plans to continue exercising once a week.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies nasal congestion, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Reports bilateral ankle swelling near the end of the day that resolves by the next morning.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure today: 156/94 mmHg.
Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, reported as stable and previously noted.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities.
Other examination findings: Otherwise unremarkable per physician.

RESULTS
Labs: Creatinine stable; otherwise reported as good.
EKG: Normal. No evidence of coronary artery disease.
Home and clinic blood pressure readings: Running a little high over the past couple of months.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing well with good coping strategies and support system. No medication indicated at this time. Patient may call if he wishes to start medication.

2. Hypertension: Not well controlled. Increase Norvasc to 10 mg daily. Order echocardiogram and lipid panel. Discuss dietary modification and decreased salt intake.

3. Status post rotator cuff repair: Doing well. Continue home exercises. No further intervention needed; considered essentially resolved.

4. Heart murmur: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, stable and previously noted. Echocardiogram ordered as above.

5. Bilateral lower extremity edema: 1 to 2+ pitting edema, likely related to dietary salt intake. Dietary counseling as above.

Patient has no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and peripheral vascular disease.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a [age not stated; DOB 03/05/1946] female presenting for follow-up. Patient reports she is "same, pretty good." She received a prior letter regarding lab results; her A1c was 9.9 and blood sugars are not well controlled. Patient reports she has remained on glimepiride 2 mg and had not increased the dose. Dose was increased per the prior plan: patient instructed to take two 2 mg tablets (4 mg) twice a day using medication currently at home, with a new prescription for 4 mg tablets, one tablet twice a day. Patient has just filled her current prescription.

Diet: Patient reports she avoids pasta, rarely keeps bread in the house, and buys wheat bread when she does. She usually has two slices of bread in the morning. Occasionally eats peanut butter sandwiches. Denies regular soda; drinks club soda and seltzer water, does not drink plain water. Counseled to reduce the number of bread slices per day.

Eye care: Sees an optometry group (Liberty Road); has had recent cataract surgery with a healing period and new glasses. Patient is seeing Dr. Sanchez. Reports dissatisfaction with one lens; the other eye is good. Physician noted possible laser treatment, pending the surgeon's assessment.

Hypertension: Patient reports a home reading of 116 systolic a couple of weeks ago. Patient reports taking all current antihypertensives. Current medications: metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide 20-25 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily.

Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease: Tolerating atorvastatin (no tolerance issues reported). Reports bilateral feet discomfort ("feel like hell") constantly, leg discomfort limiting walking, and pain extending to the hips and upper legs. Patient is attempting to walk more. Physician assessed these as relatively stable.

Tobacco: Patient is a current smoker and reports she is not ready to quit; states she will think about it.

Urinary: Reports slower urinary stream, which she attributes to age; stable per patient. Urinates several times per day. Nocturia occasionally (about once in a while). Patient notes she drinks fluids in the evening.

Skin/foot care: Patient applies a foot cream or scrub after showers when she remembers; a friend recommended one.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
Neurologic: Denies headaches and dizziness. Reports feet and leg symptoms as above.
Eyes: Reports partial dissatisfaction with vision in one eye following cataract surgery; other eye good.
Respiratory: Reports recent congestion with cough, productive of relatively clear sputum; cough improved this morning. Denies shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea, vomiting, and GI symptoms.
Genitourinary: As per HPI (slower stream, frequent urination, occasional nocturia).
Musculoskeletal: Reports leg pain and difficulty walking, and pain to hips and upper legs.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Carotids normal.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, normal rate, crisp S1 and S2. No murmurs.
Respiratory: Lungs clear; no rales or wheezing.
Extremities: No edema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable bilaterally. Thickened toenails. Mildly dry skin. No skin breakdown. Mildly decreased sensation to light touch at the tips of the first and second toes.
Blood pressure recheck in clinic: 140/60 mmHg.

RESULTS
Prior A1c: 9.9.
Blood pressure (clinic recheck): 140/60 mmHg.
Labs (blood work and kidney function) ordered today; results pending.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 diabetes mellitus, poorly controlled (A1c 9.9 previously):
- Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice daily. Patient to use current 2 mg tablets, taking two tablets twice daily until new 4 mg prescription is filled; new prescription for 4 mg tablets, one tablet twice daily.
- Continue metformin.
- Counseled on hypoglycemia symptoms (weakness, shakiness, sweating) and to report them.
- Reduce bread intake; continue avoiding pasta and sugary drinks.
- Recheck blood work today.

2. Hypertension:
- Continue metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide 20-25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily.
- Home readings improved; clinic recheck 140/60.

3. Hyperlipidemia with peripheral vascular disease:
- Continue atorvastatin (high dose) for arterial protection.
- Continue walking as tolerated.
- Leg and hip pain assessed as relatively stable.

4. Peripheral neuropathy:
- Mild decreased sensation at toes. Keep feet moisturized. Prescription neuropathy medication available if symptoms worsen; patient is currently on multiple medications.

5. Tobacco use:
- Current smoker, not ready to quit. Counseled on cessation; patient will consider it.

6. Cough/congestion:
- Recent congestion with mostly clear sputum; cough improved today. Lungs clear on exam.

7. Lower urinary symptoms:
- Slower stream and frequent urination, stable per patient. Advised regarding evening fluid intake.

8. Cataracts, status post surgery:
- Vision improved in one eye; patient dissatisfied with the other lens. Physician to follow up with surgeon regarding possible laser treatment.

Follow-up: Return in 4 months. Continue all other medications unchanged.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male here for follow-up after an emergency room visit. On Saturday, while playing tennis in very hot, humid weather, he became very short of breath after about a half hour and was struggling to breathe. He thought he was having a heart attack and became very nervous. His wife took him to the ER, where everything checked out, but he was very upset about the episode. About six hours after returning home, he felt very light-headed and dizzy. On Sunday he felt fine. He is taking all of his heart failure medications as prescribed and is in touch with his doctor. Other than the Saturday episode, he reports doing well. He reports dietary discretion: he tries to avoid junk and salty foods but admits to occasionally eating salty foods.
Cataract removal was performed three months ago and he reports no problems since then. Skin cancer was removed about five months ago and it has healed well with no problems since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for vision problems.
Positive for shortness of breath and light-headedness/dizziness during the Saturday episode, as described above. Otherwise, not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure is elevated at this visit. ER report also documented elevated blood pressure.
Neck: very supple; no jugular venous distention.
Cardiovascular: regular rate and rhythm; no murmur.
Lungs: fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: trace lower extremity edema in both legs.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable. Shows left ventricular hypertrophy, which the physician attributes as a cause of his congestive heart failure.
Echocardiogram: Left ventricular pumping function is slightly reduced but stable.
Skin biopsy pathology: Reviewed; complete removal of the lesion, and everything is reported as fine.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute exacerbation of congestive heart failure, likely precipitated by dietary sodium indiscretion with resulting fluid retention. Shortness of breath at the emergency department is attributed to this exacerbation. Findings of fine bilateral crackles and trace bilateral lower extremity edema are consistent with extra fluid volume. Elevated blood pressure was noted and will be discussed further.
   - Prescribe furosemide (Lasix) 80 mg by mouth once daily as an extra dose.
   - Start carvedilol 25 mg by mouth twice daily.
   - Nurse to see patient today.
2. Status post cataract removal three months ago, doing well; no medication changes needed.
3. Status post skin cancer removal five months ago, healed well with pathology reviewed and no further concerns; no medication changes needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back injury, approximately four months in duration.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a adult male who injured his lower back about four months ago while moving boxes when his son was moving out of a college dorm. He has not improved and was seeking care now because urgent care appointments were backed up. He tried physical therapy at his gym without significant benefit. He reports a sharp pain with turning or rolling over in sleep that resolves with repositioning. He has had episodes of near-falling with a sensation that he could not support his upper body weight, accompanied by transient tingling in the right toes that resolved after about an hour and has not recurred. He reports no current numbness or tingling in the feet. He has mild leg weakness only when carrying heavy items and feels nervous about carrying heavy objects. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen, with ibuprofen providing slightly better but shorter relief, and has tried heat and ice without benefit. He has had no gastrointestinal upset from ibuprofen. He was seen at urgent care, where an MRI was recommended; he did not pursue it previously due to insurance concerns, and he now wishes to proceed. He denies bladder or bowel symptoms, including incontinence or urinary retention.

Past medical history is notable for right total knee replacement in spring 2020, which he reports has gone well with rehabilitation, with the knee feeling about 95 percent.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever or chills.
Neurologic: Transient right toe tingling and near-falling sensation as described above, now resolved; mild leg weakness only with heavy lifting. Denies current numbness or tingling.
Genitourinary/GI: Denies bladder or bowel symptoms, incontinence, or inability to void.
Musculoskeletal: Lower back pain with turning and rolling in sleep, as described above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Afebrile. Blood pressure approximately 117/56. Heart rate 68. Oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air.
Neck: Bony protuberance at C5-C6. Nontender to palpation.
Lumbar spine: Nontender to palpation. Decreased flexion and extension. Positive straight leg raise. Paraspinal muscle spasm.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremity strength equal bilaterally.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine X-ray (obtained prior to visit): No acute bony abnormality; no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute lumbar disk herniation, suspected, based on persistent symptoms and positive straight leg raise, after lifting injury approximately four months ago. Differential includes cervical arthritis and/or residual lumbar injury, given the C5-C6 bony protuberance.
- Order lumbar spine MRI to further evaluate soft tissue structures.
- Continue physical therapy; referral placed to physical therapist through health system.
- Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg orally once daily for pain. Patient had no questions.
- Discuss further treatment options, such as epidural steroid injection, if herniation is confirmed, to be addressed at a later visit.

Patient verbalized understanding and had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain and swelling after a landscape brick was dropped on the foot yesterday.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a adult male referred by his primary care provider after dropping a landscape brick on his right foot yesterday while doing yard work. He reports soreness at the time of injury and continued working on the foot afterward. Swelling has since developed, prompting referral. Pain is rated 11 out of 10. He reports the whole right foot has been numb for a long time. He has not taken any medications for the pain and has been "toughing it out." Patient reports prior right ankle fracture about twenty years ago treated with casting, with intermittent soreness and swelling since then. He also reports intermittent soreness of the other ankle, which has been surgically treated in the past, and occasional giving way; he is unsure whether this is related to the current injury.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for right foot pain, swelling, bruising, and numbness of the entire right foot. Positive for intermittent soreness and swelling of the right ankle and intermittent soreness of the left ankle with occasional giving way. Otherwise not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals reported as within normal limits.
Right foot: bruising on the plantar and dorsal aspects; swelling; tenderness to palpation of the midfoot.
Neurovascular: capillary refill brisk, less than 3 seconds. Strong, bounding dorsalis pedis pulse, matching bilaterally. Motor and sensation intact in the right foot.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray: dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal; 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases; presence of bony fragments.
MRI of the right foot ordered to assess ligamentous injury; to be performed today at an outpatient facility in the same building.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right foot pain due to Lisfranc fracture (second metatarsal base fracture with tarsometatarsal involvement), per physician assessment based on exam and X-ray.
- MRI of the right foot ordered to evaluate for ligamentous injury; patient to be scheduled this afternoon.
- Surgical management recommended, most likely required: open reduction and internal fixation with plates and screws to restore bone alignment and ligament healing, reducing risk of loss of arch, flatfoot, and arthritis.
- Planned outpatient same-day surgery tomorrow; discharge home the evening of the procedure.
- Postoperative follow-up at 24 hours and again at 2 weeks.
- Non-weight-bearing on the right foot for 6 to 8 weeks, using crutches and in a cast; weight-bearing to be advanced gradually based on healing and tolerance.
- Patient asked about remaining in a cast without surgery; physician explained aligning bones with plates and screws gives the best outcome. Patient wishes to think about it and has time to decide.
- Nursing staff to complete paperwork and procedure setup if patient agrees.
2. Prior right ankle fracture and chronic intermittent right ankle symptoms; history of left ankle surgery with intermittent symptoms. Not discussed further.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Elevated and fluctuating blood pressure readings.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Thompson is a 67-year-old male with a history of essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis who presents with elevated and fluctuating blood pressures. He reports that over the past three to four weeks his blood pressure had been well controlled previously, but he has had periods of lightheadedness, slight headache, and occasional home systolic readings over 180 mmHg, which is well above his prior readings. He has checked blood pressure both during lightheaded episodes and when feeling well; readings were on the high side during the lightheaded episodes. He denies recent syncope. He reports intermittent chest heaviness, not sustained, and denies respiratory difficulty. He reports feeling unsteady with dizziness and a slight headache when readings are higher. He describes the dizziness as mild fuzziness and lightheadedness rather than spinning. He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and palpitations (not usually present).

Medications: He reports taking lisinopril 20 mg twice daily, as increased at his last visit, with rare missed doses. He uses a pillbox and has tried a medication app, which he finds somewhat confusing, but reports being largely on schedule. He is taking atorvastatin. For osteoarthritis, he reports being able to golf most of the time, with reduced activity during weather changes, and uses Tylenol as needed for mild pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: lightheadedness/dizziness, slight headache, intermittent chest heaviness, mild unsteadiness.
Negative: syncope (not recently), respiratory difficulty, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, palpitations (not usually).
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General and vital signs: Not discussed.
Heart: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior; not felt to be concerning at this time.
Lungs: Mild bibasilar rales; no wheezes or rhonchi; excellent air movement.
Extremities: Trace bilateral lower extremity edema.
Otherwise described as essentially normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed. (No laboratory, imaging, or home blood pressure log values were reviewed beyond the patient's verbal report of readings over 180 mmHg systolic.)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Essential hypertension, elevated and fluctuating blood pressure, with symptoms of lightheadedness and headache: Blood pressure judged to be not adequately controlled. Increase lisinopril to 60 mg twice daily. Add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Home blood pressure checks twice daily for two weeks. Follow-up in two weeks.
2. Hyperlipidemia: Continue atorvastatin. Order cholesterol panel, CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis to assess kidney function.
3. Osteoarthritis: Continue activity as tolerated without overexertion, including walking and golfing as able. May use Tylenol as needed for mild pain.

Additional counseling: Maintain fluid intake of about 6 to 8 glasses of water daily, increasing with heat or increased activity. Limit alcohol to no more than a couple of drinks per week.

Return precautions and chest heaviness evaluation: Not discussed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Joint pain, primarily bilateral knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Janet is a 33-year-old female with diabetes and hypertension who presents with joint pain. She reports that her knees have been bothering her most. She has been doing more stair-type workouts, which she believed would build muscle and support her knees, but her knee pain has worsened. Pain is equal in both knees. She denies pain in other joints such as elbows or shoulders. She had a right rotator cuff repair about two years ago with no problems since that time. She denies foot numbness or tingling and leg swelling. She reports her blood sugars have been under control. She takes norvasc 5 mg daily and reports her blood pressure has not elevated in any way since the joint pain began, though she monitors it at home.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for paresthesias in the feet, leg swelling, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure elevated today. Neck soft, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular rate and rhythm. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Left knee: slight erythema and edema, small effusion present, decreased flexion and extension. Lower extremity strength good.

RESULTS
Left knee X-ray: normal.
Labs: White blood cell count not elevated. A1c slightly elevated, not severely so.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Joint pain, left knee (bilateral knee pain reported): Left knee X-ray normal; possible mild strain. Plan: start meloxicam 15 mg once daily for pain and inflammation, order autoimmune profile to work up left knee pain, and refer to physical therapy.
2. Hypertension: Blood pressure elevated today. Plan: continue norvasc 5 mg daily, continue home blood pressure monitoring, and send blood pressure readings to the clinic in the next couple of weeks. Patient has a home blood pressure cuff.
3. Diabetes: A1c slightly elevated, not severely so. Plan: continue metformin 500 mg twice daily on current regimen.
4. Lipid screening: Order lipid profile.

Patient agreed with the plan and had no further questions. Nurse to see patient before discharge.

Right arm pain near the wrist after a tennis injury.

Note: The transcript does not specify laterality. The patient describes pain "right here... kind of toward my wrist... this part of my arm." Laterality is not explicitly stated in the transcript and should be verified.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
43-year-old female presenting with arm pain localized toward the wrist (distal radius region). She reports the injury occurred while playing tennis: during a backhand she missed the ball, hit the top of the net, and the impact jarred her arm. Mild swelling developed after the injury. Pain is present with wrist movement. She denies numbness in the hand.

Past medical history: Allergies, treated with Flonase (fluticasone nasal).
Past surgical/trauma history: Patient began to describe a stabbing injury, then reported a fall while doing lawn work onto a rake. The transcript does not clearly establish whether this was a surgery, a stabbing, or both; this should be clarified.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: Arm pain near the wrist, mild swelling, pain with wrist movement.
Negative: Numbness in the hand.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Tenderness over the distal radius.
- Pain with direct pressure over the arm.
- Pain with arm bending, most pronounced with that motion.
- Less pain with extension (backward bending) of the wrist.
- Mild pain with flexion of the wrist.
- Pain with stress on the thumb, including thumb flexion.
Other examination findings: Not discussed.

RESULTS
X-ray of the arm: No fracture seen. No significant abnormalities; essentially normal per physician review.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Arm pain after tennis injury with no fracture on x-ray. Clinical impression is strain and probable contusion of the muscle from impact.

Plan:
- Conservative management.
- Ice for pain and swelling.
- Ibuprofen (Motrin) 800 mg three times daily with food.
- Return to clinic if no improvement within about one week for re-evaluation.
- Orders for procedures and medications placed as discussed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right-sided back pain for about one week, with blood in the urine. Referred for known kidney stone.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a female named Anna with a reported diagnosis of kidney stones by her PCP. She presents with right-sided back pain lasting about one week, which has moved down to the right lower side. The pain is described as pretty constant. She has noticed blood in her urine. She reports no real pain with urination. She took ibuprofen, which helped a little, but the pain persists. She has felt mildly nauseated without vomiting. Family history is notable for a father with kidney stones. This is her first known episode of kidney stones. She had pain over the weekend and was seen by her pediatrician this morning, who referred her here due to concern for a kidney stone. She was limited in participating in Easter activities because of pain. She reports she has not been drinking enough water.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: right-sided back/flank pain radiating to right lower side, hematuria, mild nausea.
Negative: vomiting. Fever and chills were asked about; no fever reported on exam, and patient did not report chills. Dysuria: no real pain with urination.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: no fever; blood pressure and heart rate reported as fine.
Abdomen: mild pain and tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back: right costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness.

RESULTS
CT scan: 5 mm (0.5 cm) stone... [see note below]
CT scan: stone measuring 0.5 centimeters located in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.
Pending: basic metabolic panel (BMP), urinalysis, urine culture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right kidney stone (0.5 cm, proximal right ureter), without hydronephrosis, with right flank tenderness and mild hematuria.
- Increase fluid intake as much as possible to facilitate passage of the stone.
- Prescribe ibuprofen 800 mg as needed for pain.
- Provide a strainer to strain urine so the stone can be identified when passed.
- Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture. Antibiotics will be considered based on urinalysis results if infection is suspected.
- Return visit in one to two weeks. If symptoms persist, further treatment such as lithotripsy (shock wave therapy) will be discussed.
- Patient has no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
57-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and asthma presenting with shortness of breath for about two weeks. He reports waking up short of breath and feeling short of breath on exertion. He reports coughing up blood for about three weeks, described as three to four cups a day, occurring only with coughing. He has not been seen in the emergency room or hospital for these symptoms; he attempted to obtain an office appointment but was unable to. He reports a chronic knee problem with pain but no swelling, which has been present for some time.

Diabetes: Reports home continuous glucose monitor readings with postprandial spikes well over 200 and morning fasting values around 150, for about one month. Takes metformin. Most recent hemoglobin A1c was about 7.7 per the doctor's recollection.

Hypertension: Taking amlodipine (Norvasc), but has been holding it on some days because home blood pressure has run somewhat low, sometimes in the lower 90s systolic. Clinic blood pressure approximately 120/70.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath with exertion and at night on waking; positive for hemoptysis with cough.
Hematologic: Denies bruising or bleeding from teeth or gums.
Gastrointestinal: Denies vomiting blood or bleeding from other sites.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for chronic knee pain without swelling.
Extremities: Denies calf swelling. Leg swelling not reported by patient; present on exam (see below).

She feels the medication is helping but understands her blood pressure will not be controlled until she stops drinking. She has changed to taking her medications in the morning instead of the evening.

She checks her blood pressure at home. Morning readings are lower, ranging from about 130 to 145 systolic and 95 to 100 diastolic, with some readings up to 150 systolic. Evening readings are higher at rest but decrease after she sits for a while before measuring.

Follow-up of facial rash (perioral dermatitis/rosacea), on doxycycline and topical therapy.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a female (identified as Jacqueline Miller, MRN 49282721) returning for follow-up of a facial rash. Her condition is reported as much improved, though a small amount of rash remains. She initially took doxycycline twice daily for the first two weeks with marked improvement; the pharmacist advised reducing to once daily if improving. She reduced to once daily last week and reports the rash has plateaued and is no longer improving. She stopped breastfeeding and started doxycycline at that time; she is not currently breastfeeding.

Patient had not started Elidel (pimecrolimus) because she became worried after reading about it. Physician clarified that concerns about oral immunosuppressants (high-dose, long-term use in transplant patients) do not apply to as-needed topical cream or ointment use.

Current topical regimen: sulfacetamide wash twice daily (patient reports it does not dry her out significantly) and metronidazole (Metro) cream applied immediately after washing. Patient reports no other lotions, cleansers (Cetaphil), or wipes (Neutrogena). She had previously been using clindamycin per the medication list, which is to be removed.

Insurance does not cover Elidel. Patient reports cost after insurance was about $850, including with a GoodRx coupon. Eucrisa was also considered; physician noted current pricing appears higher than previously seen. Tacrolimus ointment was selected as an alternative, and a prescription was sent to Metro Market pharmacy.

Patient asked whether tacrolimus is a steroid; physician confirmed it is a calcineurin inhibitor, not a steroid. Counseling provided on expected transient tingling, burning, or flushing after application, which is not an allergy and typically lasts seconds. Patient was counseled to avoid topical steroids on the face.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Skin: Residual facial rash, plateaued with once-daily doxycycline. Patient reports feeling sun sensitive and is taking sun precautions (hat, etc.).
GI: Physician counseled on possible upset stomach or heartburn with doxycycline; no current GI complaints documented.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Fitzpatrick skin type IV (to V). Bilateral medial cheeks with a few faint erythematous papules. Mild erythema around and beneath the nostrils.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Perioral dermatitis / facial rash, improving but not fully resolved; plateaued on once-daily doxycycline.
   - Increase doxycycline to twice daily until rash resolves, then once daily for one additional week before stopping.
   - Start tacrolimus ointment (calcineurin inhibitor, non-steroid) to affected rash areas twice daily until resolved; prescription sent to Metro Market. Discontinue Elidel from medication list (not covered by insurance).
   - Continue sulfacetamide wash; patient may wash once daily instead of twice if dryness develops (patient preference noted; physician advised reducing to once daily if dryness occurs).
   - Continue metronidazole cream after washing.
   - Once rash resolves: stop tacrolimus ointment; continue doxycycline one more week, then stop; may continue wash and metronidazole cream.
   - Hold off on restarting old products until next visit. If mild flare, may try tacrolimus alone for a couple of days; if inadequate, restart doxycycline.
   - Remove clindamycin from medication list.
   - Moisturizer: Vanicream or plain petroleum jelly; samples provided. Avoid anti-aging and plant-based products. Discuss any new products with physician.
   - Sun protection counseled; doxycycline may cause photosensitivity.
   - Not breastfeeding; counseled that breastfeeding should not occur while on doxycycline.
   - Refills: doxycycline and metronidazole cream have sufficient refills per patient and physician review.
   - Return precautions: call or send MyChart message if worsening.
   - Follow-up in approximately four weeks.
   - Additional assessment noted in physician dictation: perioral dermatitis; rosacea, including ocular rosacea. Recommend gently washing eyelids once daily with a gentle cleanser such as Vanicream; Bruder mask as needed. Patient instructions to be copied and pasted per physician.

Michelle King, DOB 05/07/1982, is a 39-year-old female with quadriplegia due to prior spinal cord injury. She was admitted to district regional hospital on 06/29/2021 and discharged on 07/02/2021. She presented with increasing spasms, lightheadedness, significant constipation, and diaphoresis. In the emergency department she was febrile with a white blood cell count of 23,000. There were concerns for a urinary tract infection, and she was treated with IV antibiotics. She had labile blood pressure, headache, and vomiting, and she gradually improved. She has a supra-pubic catheter. Cultures were obtained and reviewed, and she was discharged after clinical improvement.

The patient does not believe the illness was a urinary tract infection. She believes her constipation caused her blood pressure to rise. She had hardly had a bowel movement during the admission, and after she got home she had a large bowel movement and felt much better. She told the hospital team this, and they performed x-rays, which did not confirm it. She asked whether autonomic dysreflexia can raise the white blood cell count. The physician stated that it typically does not.

She takes Miralax daily and doubles the dose when she does not have a bowel movement. She has lactulose at home for severe constipation and reports that it takes about two days to work and is hard on her. She went to the hospital because her blood pressure was out of control, with headache and vomiting, and she could not manage it at home. She now feels back to her normal self.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for constipation, headache, vomiting, and blood pressure fluctuations during the recent hospitalization. Denies pain or discomfort anywhere at today's visit.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Chest auscultation was performed with the patient taking deep breaths. Specific findings were not stated in the transcript. The patient denied any pain or discomfort.

RESULTS
Admission white blood cell count: 23,000, elevated.
Urine cultures: reviewed by the physician and described as not very impressive.
Imaging: plain x-ray only; no CT scan was performed.
Prior white blood cell count: normal last year per physician review; recently mildly elevated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute-on-chronic constipation with recent autonomic dysreflexia-related blood pressure changes. The patient believes constipation, not urinary tract infection, drove the hospitalization. The physician agrees this may be the explanation. Hot, humid weather in late June may have contributed to dehydration and worsened constipation. Plan: continue daily Miralax, use lactulose as a rescue medication as previously prescribed, and maintain hydration.

2. Leukocytosis. The physician considers inflammation from a backed-up bowel a possible cause. Plan: return in two to three weeks for fasting labs, including a repeat CBC to confirm the white blood cell count is trending down, and a full lipid panel, since it has been a while. If the count remains elevated, further evaluation of bowel issues would be considered.

3. Quadriplegia due to prior spinal cord injury. Physician noted that the patient is high risk. No additional changes were discussed.

4. COVID-19 vaccination status: unvaccinated. The patient is hesitant, citing unknown side effects, reports of "vaccine injury," and her belief that she is young and healthy. She also takes vitamin C and multivitamins. The physician recommended vaccination, stating it is the only proven preventive measure against COVID-19, that supplements are unlikely to prevent it, and that she should be considered high risk because of her quadriplegia. The physician acknowledged rare vaccine side effects, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, and discussed current treatment options. The patient was encouraged to consider the recommendation and to contact the office with questions. Decision remains with the patient.

Follow-up: return in two to three weeks for labs and reassessment.

Right index finger pain and stiffness following hyperextension injury in a motor vehicle accident in March of this year. Second opinion requested.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez, date of birth 1/12/71, is a 50-year-old male, referred for a second opinion regarding the right index finger. He was a passenger in a rear-ended vehicle, struck multiple times, in March of this year, and felt that his right index finger was stretched or hyperextended when he felt his hand was pinned under his finger. Pain has persisted since the accident, with swelling that remains present. He reports that he cannot make a fist, and that pain is sometimes unbearable, including with driving.

He was seen at Point May Orthopedics, where he was treated largely by physical therapy staff and a PA. He was offered an injection of the A1 pulley region but declined steroid injection because of a prior reaction to dexamethasone, which causes his heart to race. He was scheduled to see Dr. Alice Davis, but it does not appear he attended. He underwent an MRI of the finger for concern of capsular strain, with possible rupture of the FDS tendon. He reports that the orthopedic provider later declined injection because of the tendon tear and recommended against surgery, and that occupational therapy advised against repetitive rubbing and hand use. He feels he has not been receiving adequate medical care. He is right-handed and works as an x-ray technician, and states he needs use of his hand.

He reports a prior reaction to methylprednisolone with itching.

RESULTS of MRI (outside, 4/24/2021) are summarized below under RESULTS.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for right index finger pain, swelling, stiffness, inability to make a fist, and numbness of the index finger on examination. Positive for itching with methylprednisolone in the past. Negative for diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Positive for hypertension, treated with a blood pressure medication. Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Pleasant, cooperative, healthy-appearing male in no distress. Regular rate and rhythm. 2+ radial pulse. No swelling or bruising noted, except bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases. Slightly diminished sensation over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in 10-degree PIP flexion. Pain with pressure over the index finger, reduced with pressure at a different location. Patient reports some numbness. Pain with active flexion of the index finger, and pain at the MCP flexion crease with attempted flexion. Patient reports tearing sensation with flexion.

RESULTS
Right hand X-rays, four views, today: No bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout lesser digits, no concerning soft tissue shadows, no arthritis.

MRI right index finger, 4/24/2021 (outside facility): Focal soft tissue swelling over right index MCP joint. Partial-thickness tear of right FDS tendon. Fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of index MCP joint intact, as is the MCP joint capsule. Extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger. Partial-thickness tear of one slip of the FDS tendon (the less important of the two flexor tendons; FDP intact). Scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS tendon are thought to block excursion of the other tendons through the pulley. Extensor tendons and collateral ligaments intact.

Plan:
1. Right index finger trigger finger injection performed today. Initial attempt with one cc Celestone (betamethasone) and half cc lidocaine was not completed due to a severe painful reaction to needle introduction with hand contortion and withdrawal; needle was withdrawn and the patient counseled on the importance of getting steroid into the flexor tendon sheath. Second attempt with one cc Celestone and half cc lidocaine was performed using the same technique. Small palmar vein bled a scant amount, cleaned, and a bandage applied. Patient reassured that no harm was done to the finger.
2. Post-injection: apply ice this evening and take ibuprofen.
3. Outpatient physical/occupational therapy once a week for six weeks, with active and passive range of motion as the goal and no restrictions. Patient advised to check in with therapy weekly for accountability.
4. Patient advised to actively move the finger; a splint is not recommended as it immobilizes the finger. Patient advised that the injection is expected to reduce pain within three to five days, with further improvement over the next couple of weeks, and that repeat injection may be needed.
5. Patient counseled that he is unlikely to further tear or break anything with movement, and that the finger will be stiff and sore but can improve with therapy.
6. Patient cleared to drive.
7. Avoid dexamethasone. Note prior reaction to methylprednisolone (itching).

The shunt setting will be left unchanged for two to three months.

The patient asked whether he will be able to drive again. The doctor stated it is unlikely his movement speed will improve enough to pass the driver safety evaluation at this time, but some patients improve over nine to 12 months and he could be re-evaluated then. Neurological: Significant for continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, and hallucinations.

She denies any direct or associated trauma, including falls or known impact to the shoulder. She reports prior shoulder pain only as occasional aches and pains that responded to Tylenol. The pain is isolated to the left shoulder. Pain is constant and is worse with reaching, lifting, and attempting to raise the arm overhead. She cannot lie on her left side because of pain, and pain increases when sleeping directly on the shoulder. She has been taking Tylenol (two extra-strength tablets every six to eight hours), which helps. Pain is rated 3/10 without Tylenol at baseline, 7/10 without Tylenol at its worst as stated, and 2 to 3/10 with Tylenol.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness or tingling in the left arm or hand.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals reviewed by physician and reported as within normal limits.
Left shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. Tenderness of the greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the sternoclavicular or clavicular joints.
Bilateral hand grip is good.
Neurovascular exam of the left arm: capillary refill brisk, less than three seconds. Motor and sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Left shoulder x-ray: No fracture or bony abnormality identified.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left shoulder pain, most likely rotator cuff tendinopathy. Physician explained that the tendons attaching the shoulder muscles have been injured.
- Order MRI of the left shoulder to evaluate for other pathology.
- Referral to physical therapy for approximately six to eight weeks.
- Continue Tylenol as needed (p.r.n.).
- If symptoms do not improve, consider steroid injection of the left shoulder.
- Conservative approach to treatment. Patient asked whether the pain will resolve; physician expressed belief that the pain will improve, noting many patients respond well to physical therapy.
- Nurse to provide paperwork.
- Follow-up in approximately two weeks.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations. New patient visit.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 49-year-old man (DOB 3/2/1972) with hypertension and palpitations, referred for evaluation after an emergency room visit in March for high blood pressure and palpitations. Patient reports that on that day he had several cups of coffee and no breakfast, and he believes the episode was more likely a panic attack. He has not had recurrence of the symptoms since.

He reports blood pressure problems since childhood and a family history of hypertension. He recently saw a new primary care physician, who started a new medication about one month ago. He is currently taking Benicar HCT (olmesartan/hydrochlorothiazide 40-25) and amlodipine 10 mg daily. He refers to the hydrochlorothiazide as his "water pill."

Home blood pressure monitoring daily each morning shows readings of approximately 146 to 155 systolic. He has not yet reached the 120s. He reports trying to reduce salt intake and says he is not eating too much salt. He reports walking on a treadmill when able.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for recurrent palpitations since the March emergency room visit. Otherwise not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Patient examined using general physical exam template.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal per physician.
Respiratory: Lungs normal per physician.
Abdomen: Palpated; patient reported no tenderness anywhere pressed.
Extremities: Ankles and feet inspected for swelling; no swelling noted ("looks good").
Other systems: Not discussed.

RESULTS
Potassium one week prior: 4.0. Repeat potassium not obtained in the past week per patient.
Home blood pressure: approximately 146 to 155 systolic, daily morning readings.
Thyroid profile from March 1, 2021: referenced in request to copy forward; results not discussed in transcript.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Resistant hypertension. Patient is on three medications at maximum dose with blood pressure still not controlled. Possible secondary causes discussed, including primary hyperaldosteronism. Plan to start spironolactone. Risks discussed: electrolyte disturbances (including hyperkalemia and hyponatremia), dehydration with dizziness, and gynecomastia (rare; discontinue medication and notify physician if it occurs). Patient is willing to try spironolactone. Counseled on hydration, low-sodium diet (goal under 2000 mg/day, ideally 1500 mg/day), and the DASH eating plan; American Heart Association website (heart.org) provided as a resource. Advised that regular treadmill walking (30 minutes most days) may lower blood pressure by about 7 to 10 points.
2. Palpitations, prior episode in March, likely panic-related per patient; no recurrence reported. Not further evaluated in transcript.
3. Monitoring: Metabolic panel (electrolytes, potassium, sodium) and blood pressure check in two weeks.
4. Next steps: If not controlled on spironolactone, options include carvedilol (generally avoided due to potential erectile dysfunction) or referral to the resistant hypertension clinic for evaluation of secondary causes and consideration of renal denervation (discussed; a procedure that has been shown to lower blood pressure by about 10 points, with risks and candidacy to be determined). Patient verbalized understanding and agreement with the plan.
5. Follow-up: Return in two weeks.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left flank pain consistent with kidney stone, third episode.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents with suspected kidney stone. Symptoms began approximately three days ago with left back pain that has since migrated lower, toward the groin. Pain is constant and severe, with inability to get comfortable. Patient has not yet passed the stone. Patient reports urinating and noted blood in urine this morning. This is the patient's third kidney stone episode; prior stones typically passed in three to four days. Patient has been taking Tylenol and ibuprofen with limited relief. Patient reports chills and nausea, inability to eat, and no fever.

Chronic conditions reviewed: hypertension, managed with Norvasc 2.5 mg; type 2 diabetes (A1c 7.3 at last visit), managed with metformin 500 mg. Home blood pressures checked at least three times per week, with systolic typically in the 130s, occasionally 140s, and once 150; diastolic typically 70 to 80. Patient reports home fasting blood glucose in the low 100s and taking metformin daily. Patient reports difficulty limiting salt intake, specifically french fries, and requests help with diet. Patient was previously diagnosed with blood pressure in the 180s.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Chills. No fever. Poor appetite (unable to eat).
Cardiovascular: No chest pain.
Gastrointestinal: Nausea. No abdominal pain. Back pain radiating toward groin.
Genitourinary: Urinating. Hematuria this morning.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously known.
Respiratory: Lungs clear bilaterally, no crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen: Tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back: Right costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness. Patient reported pain with palpation of the back.
Vital signs: Blood pressure elevated at today's visit, attributed by the physician to pain. Specific values not recorded in transcript.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney stone with probable associated inflammation (recurrent, third episode). Right CVA tenderness noted on exam.
- Oxycodone 5 mg by mouth every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain.
- Continue Tylenol for breakthrough pain.
- Increase fluid intake to promote stone passage.
- Provided strainer to strain urine for stone.
- Referral to urology; patient to be seen even if stone passes within the next few days, due to recurrent stones.

2. Hypertension.
- Continue Norvasc 2.5 mg daily. No changes made given home readings.
- Patient to continue home blood pressure monitoring.
- Patient counseled on reducing sodium intake to approximately 2300 mg per day.
- Referral to dietitian/nutrition.

3. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Continue metformin 500 mg.
- Continue home glucose monitoring before meals.
- Referral to dietitian/nutrition.

Patient verbalized agreement with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction; pre-operative evaluation for planned right knee replacement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a female, date of birth 09/18/1949, with chronic congestive heart failure with diastolic dysfunction. Bmp was noted to be 3,000 in March and rose to 6,000 in April, at which time she was increasingly dyspneic. Furosemide was changed to torsemide 20 mg by mouth daily. Patient is not on a potassium supplement. Lisinopril was increased to 10 mg daily in March. Patient is interested in right knee replacement this summer at East Metro and was advised to optimize cardiovascular status before surgery.

Patient reports weight loss of about 3 to 3.5 pounds since last visit in April, which she notes may partly be water weight. She reports improved urinary urgency since starting oxybutynin. She had leg cramps the other day on waking, both legs, which resolved after drinking about 4 ounces of pickle juice. She reports heartburn that was severe for a period; she took Prilosec for about two weeks in January and has had no problems since, and she has since returned to her prior stomach medication. Patient is scheduled for knee surgery on the 24th.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for leg cramps (resolved) and urinary urgency (improved). Positive for heartburn (resolved, currently without symptoms). Patient reports that bowel and bladder function are good. Breathing is non-labored per assessment. No other systems discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General physical exam performed. Lungs sound pretty good on auscultation after deep breaths. Breathing is non-labored.

RESULTS
- Hemoglobin: within normal limits; anemia previously noted and stable.
- Potassium: 3.9, holding steady on torsemide.
- Creatinine: 0.7.
- BUN: 23, possibly slightly elevated.
- Magnesium: 1.7, normal per lab but below the target of approximately 2.
- Blood glucose: 169 mg/dL today, non-fasting.
- Last A1c: 5.5 in March (per doctor in visit); assessment later references A1c of 5.1.
- Blood pressure: reported as looking good.
- Bmp trend: 3,000 in March, 6,000 in April. Repeat results pending.
- Prior chest x-ray: recent, does not need repeat.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chronic congestive heart failure, mixed presentation. Prior exacerbation in spring. Switched from furosemide to torsemide with symptomatic improvement; weight down about 3 to 3.5 pounds. Breathing non-labored. Repeat EKG today. Continue current regimen. Labs reviewed; creatinine appropriate. Start magnesium supplement, twice daily, to target approximately 2. Follow up pending BMP results.

2. Pre-operative examination for right knee replacement, planned for end of June (scheduled on the 24th). Pre-op check to be completed within two weeks of surgery, during the first or second week of June. Hold clopidogrel for one week before surgery. Repeat EKG today if needed. No repeat chest x-ray or blood work needed today. Referral to Dr. Martin at County Surgical Services, or alternatively Valley Medical in Springfield.

3. Screening colonoscopy, overdue, no family history of colon cancer. Patient requests earlier completion due to possible change in husband's insurance. Request placed for County to be done within the next 30 days; may be completed at Bartley Regional (transcribed as "rightley regional"). Colonoscopy should not delay knee surgery. Patient may have it done at location of her choice; physician will call to arrange.

4. Diabetes/elevated blood glucose. A1c 5.1 on last check per assessment (5.5 in March per discussion). No A1c needed today. Repeat A1c may be needed before surgery.

5. Anemia, previously noted. Hemoglobin stable. Continue iron supplement (patient confirmed taking iron supplement).

6. Heartburn, resolved. Currently not requiring treatment beyond prior medication.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after acute on chronic congestive heart failure exacerbation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is an 82-year-old male with past medical history significant for hypertension and stage three chronic kidney disease who presents for hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic CHF exacerbation. Patient reports that he noticed ankle swelling while trying to follow dietary advice. One day he became significantly short of breath and called 911; paramedics placed him on a breathing mask. In the emergency room, he was told his blood pressure was very high. Per the doctor, the blood pressure recorded in the hospital was 200/90. Patient reports he takes his medications most of the time but occasionally misses a dose or two. He acknowledges dietary indiscretion, including frequent pizza and chicken wings at weekend parties. Patient was hospitalized for a couple of days, during which he received a medication that caused significant diuresis and a diuretic administered intravenously. He believes he was started on different blood pressure medications. Since discharge, he reports feeling much better, is adhering to dietary instructions and medications, and has been checking his blood pressure at home with a newly purchased cuff about every other day, with readings reported as good.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: Ankle swelling and shortness of breath preceding hospitalization (resolved per patient).
Negative: Current shortness of breath, trouble sleeping, and chest pain. Patient reports he can get up and move around without difficulty and takes a good afternoon nap.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/72. Heart rate approximately 79. Respiratory rate 26 (noted by physician as likely related to conversation). Oxygen saturation 99%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Cardiac: Two out of six systolic ejection murmur, previously heard and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram: Preserved ejection fraction of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, and mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.
Hospital blood pressure: 200/90 (as reported by physician).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure (acute on chronic exacerbation): Attributed to dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension. Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily. Continue low-sodium diet and avoid salty foods; reduce pizza and chicken wings. Weigh daily and call physician if weight gain of about 3 pounds in 2 days. Referral to nutritionist for dietary education.
2. Hypertension: Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily and Norvasc 5 mg once daily. Renal artery ultrasound ordered to evaluate for secondary causes of hypertension.
3. Chronic kidney disease, stage 3: Obtain laboratory work to assess tolerance of current regimen.

Follow-up: Return in three months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Uncontrolled hypertension, referred by new primary care physician for specialist evaluation; PCP also noted a concern on recent blood work regarding kidneys.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a adult who started seeing a new PCP last year. The PCP has made medication changes and added medications for elevated blood pressure. Patient reports adherence to medications, stating she is now taking them consistently. Blood pressure remains difficult to control. Patient has been monitoring blood pressure at home with an electronic arm cuff several times a week, with readings trending higher; the most recent home reading was 170/90. PCP increased medications after that reading. Patient reports mild headaches when blood pressure is high. She notes she is still busy at work and feels fine most days. Patient reports she no longer sees public blood pressure machines at CVS since the pandemic; doctor advised she may verify this with the pharmacy on Main Street.

Diet: Patient reports a diet high in pizza, wings, and subs, particularly during football season. She is trying to reduce intake, especially on non-game days. Doctor recommended a new restaurant on Fifth Street.

Alcohol: Patient reports about a couple of beers during the week and one or two on weekends.

NSAIDs: Patient uses ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) occasionally, not daily, for knee or back pain.

Current medications (per intake form and patient confirmation): amlodipine (Norvasc) 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice daily. Patient reports previously taking lisinopril, with later adjustments.

Family history: Both parents have hypertension; one parent had kidney disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: Mild headaches with elevated blood pressure; intermittent lower extremity swelling after prolonged standing.
Negative: Chest pain, shortness of breath (including with exertion).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 169/74. Heart rate 88. Oxygen saturation 98%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiovascular: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Uncontrolled hypertension, likely multifactorial. Medication changes may be needed; will coordinate with PCP. Before further medication changes, evaluate for a specific secondary cause:
   - Renal artery ultrasound to evaluate for renal artery narrowing.
   - Repeat urine collection, morning aldosterone level, renin level, and 24-hour urine to evaluate for adrenal causes.
   - Start cardura (doxazosin) 4 mg once daily.
2. Lifestyle modifications:
   - Decrease alcohol intake to about one to two drinks per week.
   - Reduce dietary salt intake.
   - Referral to nutritionist for dietary changes.
   - Discontinue NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen); use acetaminophen (Tylenol) for pain.
3. Home monitoring: Record all home blood pressure readings, ideally at the same time each day, and bring to the office in three weeks.
4. Follow-up: Return in three weeks. Physician will communicate plan to the patient's PCP.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for coronary artery disease, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease. Patient also reports dizziness on standing quickly and low mood.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male seen approximately three to four months after his last visit. He reports he is doing okay and that his medications are helping, though he is concerned about the number of medications he takes. He had a heart attack about six months ago, with a stent placed in the left anterior descending artery. He is taking aspirin, Brilinta, and fish oil. He reports that when he stands up quickly he becomes very dizzy; the doctor attributed this to metoprolol, which may take time for the body to adjust to, and advised against standing up too quickly. Patient asked about stent duration; the doctor stated stents are permanent, aspirin will be lifelong, and Brilinta will continue for another six months. Patient asked about stent replacement; the doctor stated stents can narrow over time and advised reporting any chest pain or exertional shortness of breath. Patient has diabetes, which he believes contributed to his heart attack. He was asked to follow up with a dietitian and has not yet done so. Patient reports fasting glucose around 130 and recalls his hemoglobin A1c as close to 16, which he states was not where he wanted it. Patient completed a blood test as requested. Doctor reviewed creatinine, which is stable after prior contrast dye exposure. Patient reports his last nephrology visit was about one year ago. Patient has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Patient has stopped taking NSAIDs (Motrin, Advil) and was advised Tylenol for headaches. Patient requests medication refills. Patient reports feeling down since his heart attack, with feelings of loneliness; he lives alone with his dog. He denies thoughts of harming himself or others. He is retiring.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for dizziness on standing quickly, low mood, and bilateral leg puffiness (patient confirms). Patient denies thoughts of harming self or others. Chest pain and shortness of breath were not specifically reported as current symptoms.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure approximately 127/80. Vital signs described as good.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Heart: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base; previously noted per doctor.
Extremities: 1+ nonpitting edema in the lower extremities. No evidence of fluid retention per doctor.

RESULTS
Creatinine: Stable, reviewed by doctor.
Hemoglobin A1c: Patient reports approximately 16 (unverified; repeat ordered).
Fasting glucose: Patient reports approximately 130.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease, status post heart attack with LAD stent (about six months ago): Doing well per doctor. Continue aspirin (lifelong), Brilinta (six more months), metoprolol 50 mg daily, Crestor 40 mg daily, and fish oil. Refills provided for metoprolol, Crestor, and aspirin. Referral to cardiac rehabilitation. No stress test indicated at this time. Patient to report any chest pain or exertional shortness of breath. Dizziness on standing likely related to metoprolol; advised to stand up slowly.
2. Stage 3 chronic kidney disease: Creatinine stable. Avoid NSAIDs; Tylenol for headaches. Doctor to contact Dr. Miller to schedule nephrology follow-up.
3. Diabetes mellitus: Hemoglobin A1c to be reordered. Referral to dietitian for diabetic education. Doctor to discuss insulin regimen with primary care physician.
4. Low mood / difficulty adjusting after heart attack, possible mild depression: Patient denies suicidal or homicidal ideation. Referral to psychiatry placed. Patient agreeable.
5. Medication refills: Sent to patient's chosen pharmacy.
